Bridge to Terabithia, Katherine Paterson's novel that won the Newbery Medal in nineteen seventy-eight. Jess Aarons is a lonely, introspective fifth-grader who feels invisible and misunderstood at home and school. He harbors a secret love of drawing and music that his family deems impractical. When Leslie Burke moves in next door, everything changes. Leslie is unconventional, brilliant, and kind, and she immediately opens Jess's world to imagination and friendship. Together, they create Terabithia, a fantasy realm in the woods that they enter by swinging across a creek on a rope. Within it they build imaginary kingdoms and quests filled with moral lessons. Leslie's sudden death by drowning while Jess is away is the novel's emotional and moral center. It forces Jess to grieve, to honor Leslie's memory, and to recognize that he has been transformed by her. The novel is celebrated for its honest treatment of grief and the redemptive power of imagination and friendship. What Paterson shows is that imagination is not escapism but a way of understanding and surviving reality, and it is also a form of spiritual legacy. When Jess finally builds a bridge to Terabithia for his younger sister May Belle, he signals that he will carry Leslie's gift of imagination forward into his life. In this way, imagination becomes immortality.
